The American bullfrog (Lithobates catesbeianus) is one of the largest anurans in North America, and its life history exhibits marked sexual size dimorphism. Upon hatching from the gelatinous egg mass, the newly emerged larva weighs a mere 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserve contained within the jelly-coated egg, which measures approximately 1.5 millimeters in diameter. Egg hatching, or eclosion, occurs rapidly under warm conditions; when incubated at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the embryos hatch after just 4 days [ab = 4 days], a relatively brief period among ranid frogs. This rapid developmental onset allows the endotrophic larva to quickly transition to the exotrophic feeding stage. The free-swimming larva then enters a prolonged aquatic tadpole phase characterized by active filter feeding and steady somatic growth. During this larval period, individuals remain as gill-breathing tadpoles, progressively developing limb buds and undergoing the allometric shifts that precede the dramatic body plan reorganization of metamorphosis.

Following the larval period, which typically spans about one year under favorable thermal conditions, metamorphic climax ensues. At a sustained water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is 365 days , a duration that aligns with the species' need to attain a sufficiently large body size before the terrestrial transition. At the moment of tail resorption and gill regression, the newly metamorphosed juvenile, or froglet, measures approximately 7.00 centimeters  in snout-vent length. This size at metamorphosis is substantial compared to many sympatric ranids, reflecting the bullfrog's extended aquatic larval stage. The post-metamorphic juvenile then embarks on a period of rapid terrestrial growth. The skin keratinization that accompanies the larval-juvenile transition equips these young froglets for a more terrestrial existence, though they typically remain near permanent water bodies to avoid desiccation and to exploit the abundant invertebrate prey available in the riparian zone.

Sexual maturation in the American bullfrog occurs at different ages and body sizes between the sexes, a pattern common among anurans with male-male competition for territories. At a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females reach puberty at 3.5 years after hatching [tp = 3.5 years after hatching], requiring an extended period of somatic investment before initiating reproductive activity. In contrast, males achieve gonadal maturation more rapidly, attaining puberty at 2 years after hatching [tp = 2 years after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The body size at which females first become reproductively active reflects this protracted growth period; the snout-vent length at puberty for females is approximately 15 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15 centimeters]. This size threshold is critical, as females must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support the considerable energetic investment in egg production, with gravid females carrying large clutches that constitute a significant proportion of their body mass.

Adult body size in this species is strongly sexually dimorphic, with males typically exceeding females in both length and mass despite the latter's later maturation. The ultimate snout-vent length for males reaches 15.2 centimeters [Li = 15.2 centimeters], while females attain a slightly larger ultimate snout-vent length of 16.2 centimeters [Li = 16.2 centimeters], a reversal of the common anuran pattern that is well-documented in bullfrog populations. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight for females can reach 800 grams [Wwi = 800 grams], with the largest individuals representing truly massive anurans. Males, though shorter in body length, are notably more robust and typically heavier relative to their snout-vent length; however, their maximum recorded wet weight is approximately 737 grams [Wwi = approximately 737 grams]. This dimorphism is thought to be driven by intense male-male competition for breeding territories, where larger body size confers a distinct advantage in agonistic encounters, while females prioritize energetic allocation toward fecundity rather than somatic growth.

The reproductive output of the American bullfrog is remarkably high, reflecting its status as a highly fecund, explosive breeder. During the breeding season at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a single gravid female may produce a clutch of approximately 20,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 20,000 eggs per spawning event], and field observations indicate that females typically complete one such spawning event per year [F_R_i = one such spawning event per year]. This enormous clutch size compensates for high rates of egg and larval mortality. Maximum longevity in the wild is also considerable; under natural conditions at an average temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 16 years [am = 16 years]. This combination of early male maturation, delayed female maturity, large adult body size, and prodigious fecundity positions the American bullfrog as a highly successful invasive species in regions outside its native range, where it often dominates aquatic communities.
